metadata.title: Wait—Git Never Stores Diffs?! Here’s What It Stores Instead 🤯 #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wondered why Git doesn’t save “diffs” like most version tools? The hook: Git stores content as snapshots of files, then uses hashing + compression to avoid duplicates—so history stays fast and storage stays efficient. Under the hood, each commit points to a tree of file states, and blobs are shared across versions via their hashes. Understanding this snapshot model helps you reason about merges, performance, and why Git is so reliable at scale. metadata.title: Python’s GIL Explained: Why One Core Can’t Run Your Code Faster #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever wondered why Python threads don’t always speed up your program? The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a runtime mechanism that ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. That design makes Python simpler and safer, but it can limit CPU-bound concurrency—especially for multi-threaded workloads. In this video, we break down what the GIL is, when it matters, and how to work around it with multiprocessing or native extensions. Follow @kreggscode and drop your questions in the comments!

metadata.title: 0.1 + 0.2 Isn’t 0.3 in Code—Here’s Why (and How to Fix It) #Shorts
metadata.description: Ever added 0.1 + 0.2 and got 0.30000000000000004? That’s the classic floating-point rounding problem—small enough to seem harmless, but dangerous in real systems like billing, money, and comparisons. Computers store decimals in binary, so many “simple” numbers can’t be represented exactly, causing tiny errors that accumulate.
